Divide the mass of the hydrogen atom by the mass of one electron.

The perimeter increases at every iteration, so 33 is the minimum.

inlines.text: Prove that the index laws hold for integer indices. (Use the laws for positive integer indices.)
For example, the product of powers result can be proved in the following way for negative integer indices.

answer.short:
For non-zero bases, all five laws hold for integer indices: $a^ma^n=a^{m+n}$, $a^m/a^n=a^{m-n}$, $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$, $(ab)^n=a^nb^n$ and $(a/b)^n=a^n/b^n$.

Use positive-integer laws, $a^0=1$ and $a^{-k}=1/a^k$, including mixed-sign cases.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b\ne0$. Positive-index cases are already known. The displayed example proves the product law when both indices are negative. If either index is zero, the product law follows from $a^0=1$.

For mixed signs, let $p,q$ be positive integers. If $p>q$, positive-index factorisation gives
$$\begin{align*}a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{a^p}{a^q}\\a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{a^{p-q}a^q}{a^q}\\a^pa^{-q}&=a^{p-q}.\end{align*}$$
If $p=q$, the product is $1=a^0$. If $p<q$,
$$\begin{align*}a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{a^p}{a^pa^{q-p}}\\a^pa^{-q}&=\frac{1}{a^{q-p}}\\a^pa^{-q}&=a^{p-q}.\end{align*}$$
Commutativity covers the opposite order. Thus the product law holds for all integers.

For any integer $n$, the definition of negative powers gives $1/a^n=a^{-n}$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\frac{a^m}{a^n}&=a^ma^{-n}\\\frac{a^m}{a^n}&=a^{m-n}.\end{align*}$$
For a positive integer $n$, repeated multiplication and the established product law give
$$(a^m)^n=\underbrace{a^m\cdots a^m}_{n\text{ factors}}=a^{mn}.$$
For $n=0$, both sides are $1$. For $n=-q<0$,
$$\begin{align*}(a^m)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{(a^m)^q}\\(a^m)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{a^{mq}}\\(a^m)^{-q}&=a^{-mq}.\end{align*}$$
For positive $n$, the product and quotient power laws are already known; for zero they give $1=1$. For $n=-q<0$,
$$\begin{align*}(ab)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{(ab)^q}\\(ab)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{a^qb^q}\\(ab)^{-q}&=a^{-q}b^{-q},\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-q}&=\frac{1}{(a/b)^q}\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-q}&=\frac{b^q}{a^q}\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{-q}&=\frac{a^{-q}}{b^{-q}}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
All five index laws hold for rational indices with positive bases.

Write the indices over common denominators and use integer laws and the unique positive roots.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b>0$, and write $r=p/n$ and $s=q/m$, where $p,q$ are integers and $n,m$ are positive integers. The definition is $a^{p/n}=(\sqrt[n]{a})^p$, using reciprocals when $p<0$.

First, equivalent fractions define the same power. For a positive integer $k$, put $t=\sqrt[nk]{a}$. Since $(t^k)^n=a$ and $t^k>0$, uniqueness of the positive root gives $t^k=\sqrt[n]{a}$. Consequently $a^{pk/(nk)}=t^{pk}=(\sqrt[n]{a})^p=a^{p/n}$.

Set $x=\sqrt[nm]{a}$. Equivalent fractions and integer laws now give
$$\begin{align*}a^ra^s&=x^{pm}x^{qn}\\a^ra^s&=x^{pm+qn}\\a^ra^s&=a^{\frac{pm+qn}{nm}}\\a^ra^s&=a^{r+s},\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=\frac{x^{pm}}{x^{qn}}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=x^{pm-qn}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{\frac{pm-qn}{nm}}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{r-s}.\end{align*}$$
For the power-of-a-power law, $a^r=x^{pm}$. The positive number $x^p$ satisfies $(x^p)^m=x^{pm}=a^r$, so it is the positive $m$th root of $a^r$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}(a^r)^s&=(x^p)^q\\(a^r)^s&=x^{pq}\\(a^r)^s&=a^{\frac{pq}{nm}}\\(a^r)^s&=a^{rs}.\end{align*}$$
For the remaining laws, put $u=\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $v=\sqrt[n]{b}$. Integer laws give $(uv)^n=ab$ and $(u/v)^n=a/b$. Both $uv$ and $u/v$ are positive, so they are the corresponding positive $n$th roots. Hence
$$\begin{align*}(ab)^r&=(uv)^p\\(ab)^r&=u^pv^p\\(ab)^r&=a^rb^r,\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^r&=\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^p\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^r&=\frac{u^p}{v^p}\\\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^r&=\frac{a^r}{b^r}.\end{align*}$$
The integer exponents $p,q$ may be negative or zero, so these proofs include negative fractional indices and zero indices.

entries.description:
In Year 7 and Year 8 we introduced powers with whole number indices and developed the index laws for these powers.

We now extend our study to rational (fractional), including negative, indices.

We live in a world of very large and very small numbers. Population sizes, government spending, intergalactic distances and the size of computer memories are examples of very large numbers. Thickness of materials, circuit diagrams and subatomic particles are examples of very small numbers. Some examples of small and large numbers are:
• the time taken by light to travel one metre is approximately 0.000 000 003 seconds
• the radius of a hydrogen atom is approximately 0.000 000 000 025 metres
• the current Big Bang model of astronomy suggests that the Universe is about 13.7 billion years old.

This chapter introduces scientific notation, which is a convenient way of writing such numbers. Significant figures are also discussed.

entries.description:
Fractional indices with numerator one
We are now going to extend our study of indices by looking at fractional indices. We begin by considering what we mean by powers such as 3^{1/2}, 2^{1/3} and 7^{1/10}, in which the index is the reciprocal of a positive integer.
If a is a positive number, then \sqrt{a} is the positive square root and (\sqrt{a})^{2}=a=a^{1}.
We now introduce the alternative notation a^{1/2} for \sqrt{a}. We do this because the third index law then continues to hold, that is:
(a^{1/2})^{2}=a^{2\times1/2}=a^{1}
Keep in mind that a^{1/2} is nothing more than an alternative notation for \sqrt{a}.

When we move the decimal point 10 places to the left, inserting the zeros, we arrive back at the original number. entries.description:
Suppose that we are using a ruler marked in centimetres and millimetres to measure the length of a sheet of paper. We find that the length of the edge of the paper falls between 15.2 cm and 15.3 cm but is closer to 15.3 cm. The normal procedure is to use rounding and write the measurement as 15.3 cm.

entries.description: All measurements involve rounding to one level of accuracy or another. For example, you may read that the mass of an electron is about 0.00000000000000000000000000091093826 g. entries.description:
Notice that, to use the idea of significant figures, we must first express the number in scientific notation.
People sometimes apply the same kind of ideas to shorten a given decimal number containing many digits. This need not have anything to do with measurement. To write a number to a specified number of significant figures, first write the number in scientific notation and then round to the required number of significant figures.
